Décès de la famille Iordache à Akwesasne: Iordache family dies in Akwesasne: “A brutal reminder of the realities many Roma live”
Qui était cette famille et que dit son h: Who was this family, and what does their story say about how Roma asylum seekers are treated in Canada?
Monalisa Iordache et Florin Iordache ave: Monalisa Iordache and Florin Iordache with their children Evelin Iordache and Elyen Iordache in Toronto Photo: Courtesy of Peter Ivanyi
Les corps des membres de la famille Iord: The bodies of the Iordache family members were found in the St. Lawrence River at Akwesasne, near the American border, last Saturday. Who was this family, and what does their story say about how Roma asylum seekers are treated in Canada? La Converse investigated.
Florin Iordache est arrivé au Canada il: Florin Iordache arrived in Canada four years ago from Craiova, Romania, with his wife, Cristina Monalisa Zenalida Iordache. They settled in Toronto, where they had two children: a girl, Evelin, and a boy, Eylen. On March 29, they were supposed to report to Toronto Pearson Airport to be deported to Romania. A few days later, Akwesasne Mohawk police pulled their bodies from the St. Lawrence River, near the Canada-U.S. border.
Les proches veulent que les gens sachent: Loved ones want people to know that the Iordaches were an honest Roma family. Florin was a pianist and worked in construction and cleaning in Toronto. He came from a family of traditional Roma musicians. “I knew Florin since he was a child. We met in Italy when I was living there. I know his mother and his father. They were a family of musicians. They played music in the street, in the subway and at weddings to earn a living. They worked hard to live. They were honest,” says Emil Julien Costache over the phone. He also comes from Craiova and now lives in California. “I want Canada to know that this was an honest family, and to be sensitive to what our communities go through in Europe,” adds Marcelone Pavel, a Toronto resident who saw the family a week before they left.
Après quatre ans passés au Canada, la na: After four years in Canada, the birth of two children, two asylum claims, a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA) application rejected in 2022 and an appeal of that decision (also rejected), the Roma family was facing deportation.
Le 29 mars, au lieu de se retrouver en R: On March 29, instead of ending up in Romania, the Iordaches took a boat toward the United States. Like other asylum seekers facing a deportation order from Canada, Florin and Monalisa, along with their one-and-a-half-year-old son and two-year-old daughter, gave their last savings to a smuggler in Montréal who promised to take them to the United States through the Akwesasne reserve. Since he had brothers living in the United States, Florin decided to cross the St. Lawrence River with his family in hopes of finding refuge on the other side of the border. “His brother told him to come join him in the United States, because in Romania there are problems, there’s a lot of racism. That’s why he took the route to the United States,” explains Emil Julien Costache.
Devant la menace de déportation, certain: Faced with the threat of deportation, some people risk their lives rather than return to Europe. Two weeks before the Iordaches left, another Roma family living in Canada crossed the border through the part of the St. Lawrence River that lies within the Akwesasne reserve. That family is currently in the United States, a source in the community confirmed to us. “When smugglers tell you they’re taking you along a route to cross a border, you don’t know what that route is like. I didn’t know what the route would be like. I just knew I was going toward a safer place for my children and my grandchildren,” explains Emil Julien Costache, who entered the United States through Mexico. His son also arrived from Mexico in December with his wife, who was pregnant. She fell while crossing the border and lost her baby.
Dans la ville de Craiova se trouve un de: The city of Craiova is home to one of the largest Roma neighbourhoods in Europe. The minority there suffers from intense racism. “When members of our communities try to go to the swimming pool, they’re turned away at the entrance, because Romanians think we’re dirty. In restaurants, they refuse to serve us. You can’t take a taxi as a Roma; Romanian drivers refuse you. And you can’t get a job either. There’s discrimination when you look for work, and they know you’re Roma, people refuse to hire you. Even when Roma manage to find a job, it’s a job that doesn’t let them live decently. There’s a lot of racism against Roma in Romania,” explains Emil, a longtime activist.
« Beaucoup de Roms quittent le pays pour: “Many Roma leave the country to settle in Western European countries, but today, with the poor portrayal of Roma in major media in Europe, whenever there are problems, the Roma are always blamed. We are the scapegoat. And that’s why so many Roma want to go to Canada or the United States,” says the exile.
C’est aussi le cas de David Laurentiu Co: The same goes for David Laurentiu Cobzaru, who arrived as a Roma asylum seeker last November. Originally from Bucharest, Romania, David first left the country for Germany, where he lived for several years. “I was afraid and, at the same time, I was tired of having to prove I was a human being,” he tells us from Toronto, where he now lives. In Romania, David’s house was set on fire by one of his Romanian neighbours. He then went to Germany, where he was beaten in the street by neo-Nazis who were attacking Roma. His relatives also had their <l1>homes burned </l1>by neo-Nazis in Germany. “A neo-Nazi tried to burn down another relative’s house by pouring gas on it in the middle of the night,” adds the social worker by training.
Il est très peiné par la fin tragique de: He is deeply saddened by the tragic end of the Iordache family. David Laurentiu understands why they decided to risk their lives crossing the border by boat rather than return to Romania. The Roma asylum seeker wants people to know that there is no justice for Roma in Romania and, more broadly, in Europe. “In Romania, the laws say that everyone is equal and has the same rights, but in reality, it’s something else. Non-Roma see us as animals, not as human beings. People discriminate against us, hate us and hurt us. People here need to know that we leave Romania because of discrimination. We are beaten by the police, we are not protected by the government, and when we, the Roma, are beaten, discriminated against or wronged, nothing is done. On the other hand, when a Roma does something wrong, everyone talks about it in the media, and the entire community is blamed. For my part, I’d rather stay here and live in a peaceful society that values my rights than go back to Romania,” explains the father of the family.
L’avocat Marian Mandache a travaillé pen: Lawyer Marian Mandache worked for 20 years in Romania for a Roma rights organization, CRISS. He has argued hate speech cases against the president, the prime minister and the foreign affairs minister of Romania, as well as school segregation cases in Craiova and cases of police abuse. “This family’s fear and distress must have been so great for them to be willing to risk their lives rather than go back to Romania,” he observes.
D’après lui, le cas de la famille Iordac: In his view, the Iordache family’s case proves that Canada’s immigration system is broken. “I think we failed to understand and analyze this family’s circumstances,” he tells us. What shocks Mandache is that the assessment of the Pre-Removal Risk Assessment application concluded there was no risk in sending the Iordache family back to Romania. “Romania is a safe country for Romanian citizens, but for the Roma minority, it is not a safe country, because Roma face a great deal of discrimination and racism there. Roma are sometimes refused entry to public spaces. They are more at risk of police brutality and more at risk of being abandoned by the justice system after incidents of police brutality. Roma men are more at risk of fatal hit-and-runs than non-Roma. On top of that, Roma children are much more at risk of racial segregation in schools,” lists the lawyer, who is of Roma origin, citing a recent European Union report concluding that 50% of Roma children in Romania suffer segregation at school. “This is not a climate in which Roma can feel safe,” says the specialist indignantly.
D’après Me Mandache, les demandeurs d’as: According to Mandache, asylum seekers who immigrate to Canada often come from disadvantaged socioeconomic backgrounds. These exiles suffer racial or political persecution. Mandache notes that groups facing racial persecution are very vulnerable and often live below the poverty line. This is notably the case for many Roma asylum seekers. They have little education and little legal knowledge. “They experience racism, and that racism is very often internalized and accepted to a certain extent, and they don’t realize how dangerous it is and that it’s hitting them. When they’re rejected by employers because of their ethnicity, or when police mistreat them, these are things that have happened to them every day for years,” Marian Mandache reminds us. “Some are illiterate; sometimes they don’t understand how important it is to have access to reports. It takes money and knowledge, especially legal knowledge, to argue your case in court. These conditions lead to the loss of human lives, as we saw with this family.”
Me Mandache se souvient d’une autre fami: Mandache remembers another Roma family from Romania, in Germany, who were to be deported and did not want to go back to Romania. That family spent years confined in German customs offices without ever entering Romanian territory. The father eventually took his own life. “They weren’t equipped to fight this legal battle, and the legal and immigration system let them down. Unfortunately, I think that in the Iordaches’ case, the system failed to give them a fair assessment of their circumstances.”
D’après Jen Danch, avocate de Toronto sp: According to Jen Danch, a Toronto human rights lawyer, the irregular border crossing is a direct consequence of the Safe Third Country Agreement. “Because of this agreement, the Iordaches could not cross the Canada-U.S. border at an official crossing and could not claim refugee status in the United States either. Instead, they were forced to cross the treacherous waters of the St. Lawrence in a small, fragile boat,” she says. “What is happening in this country that Canadian children are dying trying to leave Canada to live undocumented in the United States?” continues the lawyer, who is also an advisory member of the Canadian Roma Alliance.
Elle dénonce les stratégies politiques e: She condemns the political and legal strategies the Canadian government has used over the past 15 years to keep Roma refugees from entering Canada. She cites examples of these manoeuvres, including “<l1>the Harper government’s billboard campaign in Hungary in 2013 to discourage asylum seekers from coming to Canada</l1> and the unconstitutional list of Designated Countries of Origin (DCO), adopted in 2012, which denied asylum to Roma.”
Cette liste controversée établissait un: This controversial list established a register of “safe countries” known as “Designated Countries of Origin (DCO),” whose asylum seekers were subject to different treatment because they came from so-called democratic nations. Many of the countries on the list have large Roma populations. <l1>Many denounced the law as targeting this minority.</l1> Although its application was suspended <l2>in 2019,</l2> the DCO list still has side effects, Danch believes. “Even though the DCO list has been eliminated, its racist fallout persists,” she says. The lawyer points out that since the DCO list was repealed, it is commissioners of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada who make decisions on asylum claims, unlike what happened after Bill C-31 was adopted, when political considerations took precedence. Since the list was withdrawn, more Roma asylum seekers have been able to get fairer and more equitable hearings. “However, the biased attitudes created by the DCO list, and the message it sent to Roma refugees that they are not welcome, that they are false refugees and that they are unlikely to win their cases, persist and affect Roma asylum seekers as well as the officials who process their claims.”
Plusieurs demandes de rencontres ont été: Over the past 10 years, Roma civil society organizations have submitted several requests for meetings to the Canadian government. They urge Canada to review how Roma asylum seekers are treated and, more broadly, the human rights situation of Roma populations. To date, these requests have gone unanswered. In the wake of the Iordaches’ tragedy, Roma civil society is asking the government to act and to support Roma organizations in Canada.
Me Mandache, avocat spécialisé en droits: Mandache, a lawyer who specializes in Roma rights, urges immigration authorities to “understand that asylum seekers are human beings first and foremost.” “Their decisions can often be insufficiently justified or documented. In many cases, the system can be inhumane toward these people. They are human beings, they are not monsters, and in many cases asylum seekers and refugees are not treated humanely. In this case, the question is: ‘Did the Canadian justice and immigration system treat these migrants with dignity and fairness?’” he asks.
Puis, après un moment de réflexion, l’av: Then, after a moment of reflection, the lawyer goes on to note that Saturday, April 8 is International Roma Day, which is celebrated around the world. He adds that a minute of silence will be observed at many events across the continent in memory of the Iordache family. “On this International Roma Day, we must not forget the issues we face. This tragedy is a brutal reminder of the daily lives that many Roma people live. Very difficult lives, marked by racism and violence. I think we need to take a moment to reflect and see what we can do as a society in the face of these situations,” concludes Marian Mandache.
<strong>La famille demande le rapatrieme: The family is asking for the bodies to be repatriated, and authorities are passing the buck
Plusieurs proches de la famille Iordache: Several of the Iordache family’s loved ones, as well as many Roma living in Canada, have spoken to us over the past few days. All of them are asking the Canadian government to be more sensitive to the persecution Roma face in Romania and Eastern Europe. They also spoke of the need to repatriate the bodies of the deceased to Romania. The Iordaches’ loved ones and the Roma community are collecting money at Toronto’s Roma church to help the family repatriate the bodies and give them culturally appropriate and dignified funerals. They fear that the Canadian government and the Romanian embassy in Canada will do nothing to repatriate the bodies of the four family members to Romania, where Florin’s and Monalisa’s parents wish to bury their children and grandchildren.
En attendant, le père de Monalisa, Flori: In the meantime, Monalisa’s father, Florin Caldararu, who lives in France, has asked Canadian government bodies and Romanian consular services to repatriate the bodies of his daughter, his son-in-law and their two children to Romania, in a letter of which La Converse obtained a copy. Profoundly shaken by the loss of his children, he wants only to be able to offer them a final farewell worthy of their memory.
Le ministère roumain des Affaires étrang: Romania’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, through the Romanian embassy in Ottawa, the Consulate General of Romania in Montréal and the Consulate General of Romania in Vancouver, confirms that it is “following developments related to the tragic incident” and “in contact with citizens who state that they are members of the victims’ family [to provide] consular assistance in accordance with legal authority, if necessary.”
Cependant, à propos du rapatriement des: However, regarding the repatriation of the Iordaches, the Romanian embassy and consulate say they have not received confirmation of the victims’ citizenship. “In the absence of this notification, the Romanian missions cannot take steps to facilitate the repatriation of the bodies to Romania,” Romania’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs told us by email through its diplomatic offices in Canada.
D’après des informations dont nous dispo: According to information we have, proof of identity has been sent to the embassy. It remains to be seen whether the fact that Eylen and Evelin, the Iordaches’ two children, were born in Canada is an obstacle in the processing of this repatriation request. The embassy has still not confirmed anything to us in this regard.
D’après nos sources, les corps des défun: According to our sources, the bodies of the deceased are at the Montréal morgue, and the autopsies are complete. It is now possible to release the remains for repatriation. <l1>The Quebec coroner’s office is also conducting an investigation into the deaths</l1>. At the Consulate General of Romania in Montréal, employees explained to us that the repatriation of bodies is handled by private companies that take care of the administrative tasks. It is up to the victims’ relatives to cover the bill and pay the repatriation costs, an employee who wished to remain anonymous told us.
Quant au rôle du consulat, il se limite: As for the consulate’s role, it is limited to consular services, such as providing documents and confirming identities. Several funeral homes, however, told us that the role of consular bodies on Canadian soil is to help grieving families organize a repatriation to their country of origin.
Le rapatriement d’une dépouille est un p: Repatriating human remains is a long and costly process. Various Montréal funeral homes, including Alfred Dallaire Memoria, Urgel Bourgie and Aeterna, explained to us the procedures to follow when there is a request for repatriation to a foreign country. Some funeral homes handle the entire repatriation process, but the fees for this service range from $10,000 to $15,000 per person. Authorization is also required from the countries involved (in this case, Canada must authorize the remains to leave, and Romania must authorize their arrival and burial). Finally, because the victims’ legal documents are needed, the process requires the consulate’s cooperation.
Mais une question revient parmi les proc: But one question keeps coming up among the family’s loved ones and in Canada’s Roma community: if the Canadian government was prepared to deport the Iordaches to Romania while they were alive, what does it plan to do with their remains now that they are dead? Who will bear the cost of repatriating their bodies? Immigration lawyer Peter Ivanyi, who represented the Iordache family, believes it is the state’s responsibility.
« Je ne pense pas que l’ambassade de Rou: “I don’t think the Romanian embassy will take this request as seriously,” he says. “I think that if the relatives had the means to pay for the repatriation, it would help the government facilitate the process. If they don’t have the means, I think the government should do it. I don’t think they should have been deported; so, in the current situation, I understand the feeling of some people who think that if the government was prepared to pay to deport them, why isn’t it paying to repatriate them; and ultimately, maybe it will,” says Peter Ivanyi.
Interrogé à ce sujet, le ministère d’Aff: Asked about this, Global Affairs Canada would only say that “the families and friends of those who died near Akwesasne are in [its] thoughts.” At the time of writing, Geneviève Tremblay, a spokesperson for Global Affairs Canada, confirmed to us that the department is in contact with Romanian authorities on the matter, but did not answer our question about the Canadian government’s financial contribution to repatriating the Iordache family. According to the latest information we had, Global Affairs Canada met with the Romanian embassy on Thursday morning (April 6) to facilitate the repatriation. It remains to be seen who will have to foot the bill for this tragedy.
